title: Meet Swiftiephylus, a group of insects named after Taylor Swift
excerpt: Four newly described species of Australian plant bug have been named in honor of world-famous pop star Taylor Swift.
content:
Blonde with a pop of red? Could be the superstar singer Taylor Swift. Or maybe a true bug named for her.

Scientists named the tiny, big-eyed Australian bugs to honor record-breaking, world-famous music icon Taylor Swift. This Swiftiephylus group recognizes her “show-stopping talent, heart-wrenching lyrics, and the joy and comfort she has brought to many.” That’s what researchers wrote when they described the insects September 9 in Insect Systematics & Evolution.

Explainer: Insects, arachnids and other arthropods

There are some 10,000 species of plant bugs found all over the world. Like their name suggests, they’re plant-munchers. But little had been known about their diversity in Australia.

Insect biologist Christiane Weirauch works at the University of California, Riverside. In 2022, another entomologist, Sarah Schroeder, began her PhD work with Weirauch. Some of these mystery bugs became a part of her research.

“I was really excited,” Schroeder says. “It’s a dream thing for a scientist to get to describe new species.”

Little insects, big honor

Schroeder and Weirauch studied flower-eating plant bugs found in Australia’s she-oak trees. Each bug is about the size of a head of a pin. By comparing their body shapes, colors and genes to those of known species, the researchers found 12 new species. They organized them into five groups, each containing closely related species. Each group is known as a genus. One genus — Swiftiephylus — bears a name with special meaning to Schroeder.

“I’ve been a lifelong Swiftie,” Schroeder says. “Taylor’s music has underscored so many of the major milestones of my life. So it felt authentic to me to honor her by naming these species after her and giving her a gift back for all of her music.”

Schroeder picked the four species to bear Swift’s name because of their yellow colors accented with splashes of red. “Taylor’s pretty well known for having her red lip,” Schroeder says. “And the fans affectionately call her Blondie.”

Beyond the obviously named S. taylorae, Schroeder gave the other three species Latin translations of some of Swift’s album names. S. amator is for Lover. S. intrepidus is for Fearless. And S. poetorum references The Tortured Poet’s Department.

For Schroeder, this song isn’t finished. Swiftiephylus barely scratches the surface of unknown insect life. She notes that it’s crucial to describe species in order to conserve them. You can’t protect what you don’t know is there, she explains. With possibly millions of undescribed insect species still out there, it’s a conservation problem researchers know “All Too Well.”

title: Star Power: Olivia Ryerson
excerpt: Meet Service Star Olivia Ryerson, 14. A nationally ranked chess player, Olivia runs a free girls’ chess club at her high school, in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania.
content:
Meet Service Star Olivia Ryerson, 14. A nationally ranked chess player, Olivia runs a free girls’ chess club at her high school, in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. Olivia also runs chess tournaments and donates the proceeds to breast cancer research. (And she’s a TFK Kid Reporter alumna!) TFK reader Lassya Fenning spoke with Olivia about her ongoing efforts. How do you get girls plugged into chess?

At my school, I manage an all-girls chess club where girls learn, play, and improve together. Girls make up only about 10% of tournament chess players, so my school’s Queens Club provides a community for them to develop skills. I also run a Philadelphia-based chess tutoring service for girls. S. Chess Federation tournament director. Creating a community of girls who love the game is incredibly important.

What do you enjoy about volunteering? Seeing other girls fall in love with chess is rewarding. I want girls to have the opportunities I’ve had and to share my passion for the game. What challenges have you faced? One of the biggest challenges is building a sustainable community that keeps people coming back. Also, interested girls come from many different schools and areas in Philadelphia, so logistical planning and outreach are difficult.

I’m still learning, but the rewards make it worth it. You donated funds from your chess tournaments to raise money for breast cancer research. What inspired you to do this? I’ve researched the side effects of medications used to keep breast cancer in remission—specifically how they can reduce cognitive skills and quality of life. Since chess is shown to increase cognitive function and focus, I chose to support a group called Living Beyond Breast Cancer.

It works to improve the quality of life for patients. I hope to help that mission while building a community of chess players who care. This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

title: A World Without Imagination
excerpt: TFK Kid Reporter Adam Sadi read Building 903 and interviewed its author, Lois Lowry. Lowry also wrote The Giver, a 1993 Newbery Medal–winning dystopian novel. Read Adam’s thoughts below.
content:
TFK Kid Reporter Adam Sadi read Building 903 and interviewed its author, Lois Lowry. Lowry also wrote The Giver, a 1993 Newbery Medal–winning dystopian novel. Read Adam’s thoughts below. It’s 2099, and the world is totally different: only one country, one dictator, and zero books. And there’s no imagination—because it’s forbidden! That’s life for 14-year-old twins Tessa and Theo in Lois Lowry’s new book, Building 903.

When Theo disappears, Tessa and her parents search for him. And in solving the mystery, they uncover things that their society has kept hidden. An elderly neighbor gives Tessa a key that leads to a secret stash of books. Tessa has never read or even held a book before. These unfamiliar objects hold clues to Theo’s disappearance. As Tessa discovers what stories can do, she begins to understand what people lose when they’re not allowed to read.

Building 903 is about what happens when people lose their imagination. Lowry told TFK that imagination helps us put ourselves into “the mind, the soul, the heart of another human being.” When she writes, she imagines what her characters think and feel. In real life, this same skill—empathy—helps us understand other people. Lowry leaves some work for her readers, too.

“I did leave some things unanswered, and I did that on purpose,” she says. These mysteries give kids something to discuss, and a reason to use their own imagination. Building 903 made me think about the future. Its dystopian world is scary, but the book also left me thinking about hope. If stories and imagination help us understand one another, maybe they can help us have more empathy and make better choices, too. I recommend this book to readers who enjoy mysteries and stories about different worlds and big questions.

title: Star Power: Oceane Qian-Feuillat
excerpt: Meet Service Star Oceane Qian-Feuillat, 16. As Miss New Jersey Teen USA, Oceane started a program called Girls Leading Our World (GLOW).
content:
Meet Service Star Oceane Qian-Feuillat, 16. As Miss New Jersey Teen USA, Oceane started a program called Girls Leading Our World (GLOW). The program helps girls build confidence, practice public speaking, and take on leadership roles. TFK reader Sonali Vadada spoke with Oceane about her efforts. What first inspired you to start GLOW? Growing up mixed-heritage, I struggled to find my own voice.

I wanted to create a supportive space where young girls could discover their unique strengths, embrace their differences, and feel proud of who they were. How does GLOW help girls overcome the fear of public speaking? We make it fun and encouraging! We do interactive activities where girls can practice speaking and sharing their ideas. I always tell them that having confidence doesn’t mean you never get nervous—it just means you give it a try anyway.

How do you juggle service work, school, and other commitments? I stick to a solid schedule, prioritize what’s most important, and make sure to save time for myself. Most importantly, I remind myself that perfection isn’t necessary. You just have to do your best. Can you share a moment when you realized your work was making a difference? , a nonprofit, and one participant was really shy.

She ended up building so much confidence that she modeled in a fashion show later on. , which was incredible to see. Why is it so important for kids to be involved in the community? We are the generation inheriting the future. We don’t have to wait until we grow up to make a difference. Kids can make a real impact right now, whether that’s starting a recycling club or running a neighborhood fundraiser. This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

title: Friendly Faces
excerpt: Friendship is a theme in many books. Some teach lessons in kindness. Others remind us how nice it is to have a buddy. Here are three of TFK’s favorites.
content:
Friendship is a theme in many books. Some teach lessons in kindness. Others remind us how nice it is to have a buddy. Here are three of TFK’s favorites.

Enemy Pie

Author Derek Munson’s book teaches you how to deal with an enemy. The main character does not like Jeremy, his new neighbor. Jeremy is “Enemy Number One.” Luckily, Dad knows how to deal with enemies. He cooks up some enemy pie. This secret recipe changes everything.

The Invisible Boy

How does it feel to not be noticed? Brian knows too well. No one thinks to include him. Even the teacher seems to overlook him. Classmates don’t notice that Brian is smart, creative, and kind. Then a new kid comes to school. This book by Trudy Ludwig shows the difference an act of kindness can make. George and Martha George and Martha is a series by James Marshall. The books contain short stories about two hippos who are best friends. They remind us that life is better with a pal. Readers learn the importance of being honest with friends. They learn that anything can be fun with someone by your side.

title: Do You Need It?
excerpt: A need is something you cannot live without. A want is something you enjoy. Knowing the difference can help you be money-smart. Food NEEDS Food is something people need each day.
content:
A need is something you cannot live without. A want is something you enjoy. Knowing the difference can help you be money-smart. Food NEEDS Food is something people need each day. Some kids buy school lunch. Adults buy groceries. Food gives us energy. WANTS Treats are yummy to eat. But people do not need them every day. Save up some money.

You can treat yourself once in a while. Clothes NEEDS People get dressed every day. They need clothes to wear. Shirts and pants are necessary. Shoes are too. Some kids need school uniforms. WANTS It is nice to have a lot of clothes to choose from. But you do not need too many. See what you have before buying something new.

Travel NEEDS Everyone needs to get from place to place. Kids get rides to school. Adults travel to work. Travel costs money. But travel to school and work is necessary. WANTS Travel for fun is called a vacation. People might fly on a plane. They can stay in a hotel. Vacations are special. They are not always needed.

title: Scientists Say: Abyssal Zone
excerpt: This layer of the ocean lies far out of reach of sunlight. Yet, life still thrives.
content:
Abyssal Zone, (noun, “ab-IZ-sell ZONE”)

The abyssal zone is the second-deepest zone of the ocean.

Scientists describe the ocean’s depths in five layers. The abyssal zone is the fourth layer. The abyssal zone includes both the water itself and the seafloor. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, or NOAA, says this zone begins at a depth of 4,000 meters (13,100 feet). Other experts say it starts at a depth of 2,000 meters (6,600 feet). Everyone agrees, however, that it extends to a depth of 6,000 meters (19,700 feet).

Light usually shines through the ocean’s top layer. That’s why scientists call this layer the sunlight zone. The sunlight zone ends at a depth of 200 meters (660 feet). That’s where the twilight zone begins. As you descend through the twilight zone, sunlight fades. By the time you reach the third layer — the midnight zone — all surface light is gone. This layer begins at a depth of 1,000 meters (3,300 feet). Descending below the midnight zone brings you to the abyssal zone. Below the abyssal zone lies the hadal zone.

The abyssal zone is cold, dark and under massive pressure from the water above. Temperatures remain near-freezing. Sunlight never penetrates to these depths. The only light there comes from life forms. Some living things here are bioluminescent. That means they produce light. These species often use that light to draw in prey or mates.

Animals and microbes live in the abyssal zone. One type of life you will not find there, however, is plants. They get their energy through photosynthesis, which relies on sunlight. In the sunless abyssal zone, they could not survive.

With no plants to support the food chain directly, life in the abyssal zone must rely on other food sources. Organic material drifts down from the surface. Microbes or animals may eat that material. That organic material may be tiny particles. Or it could be the body of a dead whale. Chemicals arising from deep below the Earth — such as from hydrothermal vents — may also support deep sea life.

Only a few parts of Earth’s oceans go deep enough to include all five ocean layers. The Mariana Trench is one example. This deep ocean trench lies in the Western Pacific Ocean. It descends to a depth of almost 11,000 meters (36,000 feet). Descending into this trench would take you through all five major zones of the ocean, including the abyssal zone.

title: Mission: Boost Literacy
excerpt: Join a community of kids who are making the world a better and brighter place. TFK Service Stars know that even the smallest actions can make a big impact.
content:
Join a community of kids who are making the world a better and brighter place. TFK Service Stars know that even the smallest actions can make a big impact. Mission of the Month Reading, writing, and speaking are important skills. Without access to literacy materials, such as books, people miss out on a chance to improve their communication with words. Specialized kinds of literacy, such as digital and financial literacy, give people an understanding of how the world works. All around the country, kids are aiding the spread of literacy. If you have a friend or schoolmate who’s struggling with reading and writing, ask how you can help.

Research ways to promote different kinds of literacy in your community. What groups or events need more attention and support?

Ask a school or public librarian for information about the library’s literacy programs. Is there a way you can support these efforts?

Know multiple languages? Read a book with someone who wants to learn one of them.

Stars Shine Brighter Together Reading to young children helps them develop strong literacy skills. Plus, it’s fun! Ask a teacher for permission to visit a classroom of younger students. Have your classmates help you select fun books that you can read aloud. It’s story time! Need help getting started? Talk to an adult or pair up with a friend to find an idea that feels right for you. Tell Us About It! We want to hear all about your efforts to boost literacy. Share your story with us at tfkeditors@time.com for a chance to be featured in TIME for Kids.

title: Braving the Storm
excerpt: Sisters Alone, which was published in September, is a tale of bravery and sisterhood.
content:
Sisters Alone, which was published in September, is a tale of bravery and sisterhood. The book is about “two sisters who have had a crack in their relationship ever since their mother died,” author SHIFA SALTAGI SAFADI told TIME for Kids. “When they get stuck home alone in a blizzard, they have to figure out what that crack is, and heal it. They lean on each other in order to survive the storm.”

The book is written in verse, as poetry. It has rhythm. Safadi enjoys writing in verse because of the “many beautiful things” it can do: “I love the way that verse tells a complete story with so [few] words,” she says. “I think about every single word on the page and how it makes the reader feel, how it sounds musically, how it looks on the page visually.”

title: TFK at New York Comic Con
excerpt: TFK Kid Reporter Shaiyar Dhillon attended New York Comic Con in October. In this article, he shares his experience with TIME for Kids readers.
content:
TFK Kid Reporter Shaiyar Dhillon attended New York Comic Con in October. In this article, he shares his experience with TIME for Kids readers. Every year since 2006, thousands gather at New York City’s Javits Center to take part in one of the world’s largest comic and pop culture events. My family and I have been going to New York Comic Con (NYCC) since I was about seven months old: I wore a Superman onesie.

We love to read comics and books, cosplay, and watch our favorite superhero shows and movies. For us, NYCC is an annual family celebration. Over the years, I’ve cosplayed some of my favorite characters, such as Dipper from Gravity Falls, Hunter from The Owl House, and Miles Morales from Spider-Man. I’ve also cosplayed Percy Jackson from Rick Riordan’s best-selling Percy Jackson series.

At this year’s NYCC, I got to meet Riordan, and other authors, as well. Authors Abound Randy Ribay is a National Book Award finalist who writes the Avatar: Last Airbender books. When I met him, Ribay told me he got the gig because he was both a writer and a fan. In 2020, he watched the whole series on Netflix and “did one of those long Twitter threads where I watched an episode and then would type up my reactions, my analysis of the episode.

And I did that for the entire series. Somebody [saw] that at some point, and they’re like, ‘Oh yeah, this writer is a fan. Let’s ask him.’” Pretty cool. Next up from Ribay is his third Avatar book, about Avatar Sonam. The book was announced at Comic Con. My family and I spent some time strolling through NYCC’s Artist Alley.

I got to meet Kami Garcia, who writes the Teen Titans series. I also met Zeno Robinson, who voices Goh in Pokémon Journeys and Hunter in The Owl House. He signed my Owl House graphic novel. On Sunday, the last day of Comic Con, I spoke with one of my favorite writers, Rick Riordan. You know him as the creator of the Percy Jackson universe.

Riordan was at Comic Con to chat about his new book, The Wild Zone, which came out in September. It’s the first book of the Camp Half-Blood Chronicles. Riordan was joined on a panel by series coauthors Annabelle Oh, Kyle Lukoff, Pablo Cartaya, and Jade Adia. Oh cowrote the first book in the series. During the panel, she said that main character Katie Kim is “a daughter of Aries, and she’s an underwhelming daughter of Aries.

.  She’s kind of in everyone’s shadow.” Oh added that Katie is “trying to make her way and prove herself”—just like most of us. Time to Chat After the panel, I got to sit down with Riordan and Oh and ask them questions about Camp Half-Blood: The Wild Zone. Here’s part of our conversation. Shaiyar: Can you tell me about the origins of the Camp Half-Blood series, and how you met the collaborators?

Riordan: I was on set with the Percy Jackson TV show, and we were having conversations about what we could do with the sets between seasons. That got me thinking about if there were stories that we could tell that happened between The Lightning Thief and The Sea of Monsters. I started brainstorming, and I came up with this idea: What if we had four new heroes?

And what if I could find four great other authors who could each take one of their voices and bring them to life? Shaiyar: How does it feel to write in a universe like Percy Jackson? Were you a fan? Oh: I was. I read them a long time ago, when the first book came out. Rick has such a conversational and approachable voice for readers.

It’s like you’re hanging out with a friend and the friend is just telling you a fun story. So I liked his writing style, and I enjoyed his books. When I got the opportunity to work on this, it was an honor. But it was also intimidating, because I know how beloved that world and those characters are. I had to make sure I worked very, very hard to do all of my research on the past material and to make sure I knew enough about the world that I would not let the fans down.

Shaiyar: What do you like better, working on TV or writing books? Riordan: Writing books. I mean, that’s where I live. No offense to the television industry: They do amazing work. But it’s not my world. I’m lucky that they invited me in and I got to learn more about it. But I am first and foremost always a novelist.

Shaiyar: Is there a scoop you can give us about Season 3 of the show? Riordan: All I can tell you is that I think it’s the best one yet. You should totally watch it. I think you’ll like it! This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

title: What is the Weather?
excerpt: Step outside. What is it like? The day might be sunny and dry. It might be damp and cool. That is the weather. Here are some ways to talk about the weather.
content:
Step outside. What is it like? The day might be sunny and dry. It might be damp and cool. That is the weather. Here are some ways to talk about the weather.

Temperature

This is how hot or cold the air is. We measure it in degrees Fahrenheit (ºF). At or below 32ºF is freezing. Above 85ºF is hot.

Wind

The movement of air is called wind. It can be a gentle breeze. It can be a strong gust. Wind is measured in miles per hour.

Precipitation

Precipitation is water that falls from the sky. Rain is one type. When it is cold, there might be snow. Precipitation is measured in inches.

Humidity

This is how much water is in the air. The water is not falling. People say humid days feel damp or muggy.

title: How brain-eating amoebas may wriggle into someone’s brain
excerpt: Naegleria amoebas are dogged explorers, especially in tight spaces. These behaviors might help these brain-eating microbes crawl into our heads.
content:
Some deadly amoebas may be primed to invade your brain.

Naegleria fowleri (Neg-LAIR-ee-ah FOW-ler-eye) is sometimes called the brain-eating amoeba. Normally, it lives in ponds, where it dines on bacteria. But the way it seeks out meals might also make it good at crawling up our noses — and into our brains.

Naegleria amoebas are intrepid explorers. In lab studies, they probe nooks and crannies with dogged persistence. When creeping down narrow passageways, the amoebas charge relentlessly forward, almost never turning back. “They’re like robots,” says Lillian Fritz-Laylin. “They just go and go and go.”

That’s what Fritz-Laylin’s team reported on September 10 in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. A cell biologist, she works at the University of Massachusetts Amherst. She’s also an investigator at the Howard Hughes Medical Institute.

Their persistence might help these tiny, single-celled creatures make long journeys. That includes the trek from someone’s nostrils all the way to their brain. The new work offers more insight into their behavior. “We know almost nothing about the basic biology of these organisms,” Fritz-Laylin says.

N. fowleri amoebas are typically harmless to people. They usually dwell in warm bodies of fresh water. There, they squirm through mud, hunt prey and mind their own business. But on rare occasions, one can wash up a swimmer’s nose. From there, it can migrate through the nasal cavity and into the brain. Along the way, it destroys and eats tissue.

Once in the brain, it starts to reproduce, usually with lethal consequences. The United States sees fewer than 10 Naegleria infections most years. Many occur at summer swimming spots. Nearly all are fatal.

In the lab, Fritz-Laylin’s team tested how Naegleria amoebas move through different environments. Rather than N. fowleri, they used N. gruberi. This amoeba shares behaviors with its brain-eating relative but is harmless. “It’s a lot safer to work with something that can’t kill you,” Fritz-Laylin points out.

Her team placed the amoebas on glass-bottom dishes. Through a microscope, they watched the critters move around. The amoebas seemed to be interested in exploring.

The dishes held narrow microchannels. Once the amoebas bumped into a channel opening, they very rarely left it, Fritz-Laylin reports. They squeezed through channels smaller than themselves. And those tight spaces sometimes sped them up. Inside the largest channels tested, the amoebas zipped along twice as fast as cells on the outside.

Naegleria’s persistence and need for speed may make it unique. The team didn’t observe the same behaviors in a different type of amoeba that they tested. Such skills probably make Naegleria good at hunting bacteria in pond sediments, says Fritz-Laylin.

Those same behaviors, however, could also explain N. fowleri’s dark side. Put one at “the wrong place at the wrong time,” she says, “and it can cause devastating infection.”

title: Sophia’s Shelves
excerpt: Sophia Parekh loves books. Her family’s basement is full of them.
content:
Sophia Parekh loves books. Her family’s basement is full of them. There are thousands of books for kids of all ages, from babies and toddlers to elementary schoolers and teens, on neatly organized shelves. It’s like a secret library. Since age 7, Sophia has been giving books out for free through a program she started. It’s called Sophia’s Book Stand.

“My initial goal was to send about 1,000 books a year to kids in need,” Sophia, now 13, told TIME for Kids. To date, the New Jersey seventh grader has managed to give away more than 8,000 books. In September, she was awarded a Gloria Barron Prize for Young Heroes. These are given out every year to young people who are making a positive impact on the world.

Sharing Stories To request free books from Sophia’s Book Stand, teachers and families fill out an online form. It asks for kids’ ages and interests. Sophia uses the information to scan the shelves in search of a perfect match. “I try to think of what books I was into” at different ages, Sophia says. “And I try to make sure that whoever gets these books, they definitely like them.”

To develop a love of reading, she adds, “you have to find a book that you’re into and that you can connect to.” Requests come from all over. Sophia has mailed books to a 4-year-old in Pennsylvania who loves princesses. She’s mailed them to a fifth-grade teacher in Arizona and a sister and brother in New York who are obsessed with dinosaurs and unicorns.

As Sophia’s collection has grown, so has the number of books she’s able to give. “At first, I was just sending each child two to three books,” she says. “Now I try to send between eight and 10 books each so they can build their libraries at home.” In June, Sophia gave 288 books to 36 students in Linden, New Jersey.

She wanted them to have books to read over the summer. “I’m very, very grateful to Sophia for the opportunity that she has given to my students,” teacher Elizabeth Nardone says. “To help other kids and spread the happiness of reading is just something special.” Big Dreams Many of the books Sophia gives away are supplied by people in the publishing business.

Recently, she reached out to Mary Pope Osborne, author of the Magic Tree House series. “Kids love, love, love those books,” Sophia’s mom says. Osborne’s’s publisher promised to send multiple copies. Donations come from friends, too. “Books are just so important in all our lives, but especially in children’s lives,” Lindsay Gordon Bezalel says. She and her family live across the street from Sophia.

“I’m happy to support her. She does the legwork that’s needed to make sure books are getting into the right hands.” This spring, Sophia’s Book Stand turns six. “I definitely want to expand,” Sophia says. Her goals include getting more bilingual books and books with diverse characters. She also hopes to ship books to kids in other countries. That way, she says, “everyone can get a chance to get books, no matter where they live.” Inspired? Let Sophia’s story inspire you to promote literacy in your community. title: Towering Spires
excerpt: The United States has a new national park. Chiricahua National Park is in southeastern Arizona. The historic place became a national park on October 20. Chiricahua was formed 27 million years ago.
content:
The United States has a new national park. Chiricahua National Park is in southeastern Arizona. The historic place became a national park on October 20.

Chiricahua was formed 27 million years ago. Volcanoes erupted. The volcanic ash cooled. It hardened into rock. Erosion created rock formations called hoodoos. Visitors can hike around these strange pillars.

The park contains varied ecosystems. There’s desert. There are forested areas and grasslands. Many animals call the park home. Bears, mountain lions, and birds can be seen there.

The park has a rich history. It’s the homeland of the Chiricahua Apache Native Americans. It was first protected as a national monument in 1924. Now it has been upgraded to a national park. The title recognizes the site’s importance.

Doug Burgum is the U.S. Secretary of the Interior. In a statement, he spoke about the area’s “towering rock spires.” He noted its Apache heritage and its biodiversity. Burgum called it “one of America’s most extraordinary landscapes.”
